questions.q: What is the central conflict presented in 'अपना देश' that can serve as a discussion prompt for a class debate?
questions.a: The central conflict is the tension between industrial/technological development (represented by factories, pollution, concrete) and ecological/cultural preservation (clean river, greenery, traditional lifestyle). A wrong answer like "the author dislikes his hometown" reveals the student has missed the systemic critique — they're personalizing a structural argument.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the author says "जिसे हम विकास की तकनीकी सभ्यता कहते हैं वह मिट्टी की विलासिता है" (What we call technical civilization of development is soil's luxury).
questions.a: The author means modern development consumes natural resources (soil, water, air) as if they are infinite luxuries, not necessities. It treats the earth as a disposable input. A wrong answer like "development is expensive" misses the ecological metaphor — the student hasn't grasped that 'मिट्टी की विलासिता' implies the earth pays the price for human 'progress'.

questions.q: During a group discussion, a peer claims: "The author is just nostalgic; he doesn't offer solutions." Using the text, formulate a spoken rebuttal that acknowledges the peer's point but extends the argument.
questions.a: Valid rebuttal: "हाँ, लेखक समाधान नहीं देते, लेकिन वे हमें प्रश्न करने को मजबूर करते हैं — 'हम अपनी जीवन-शैली को क्या समझते हैं?' (पैरा 7). उनका उद्देश्य समाधान देना नहीं, चेतना जगाना है।" A wrong answer that just says "You're wrong, the author shows the river dying" fails to engage with the peer's claim — it doesn't demonstrate active listening or concession-building.

questions.q: Compare the author's description of Banksa's past (clean river, birds, cool breeze) with its present (polluted river, noise, heat). What rhetorical strategy does this contrast serve in a discussion context?
questions.a: The before/after contrast functions as empirical evidence for the argument that development has degraded life quality. In discussion, it lets speakers move from subjective feeling ("I feel sad") to textual proof ("Paragraph 3 shows the river could not be crossed; now it's a drain"). A wrong answer like "It shows the author likes the past better" reduces a rhetorical device to mere preference — missing its argumentative function.

questions.q: Evaluate this discussion opening: "Friends, today we discuss whether development is good or bad. I think it's bad because the chapter shows pollution." Is this effective? Why or why not?
questions.a: Ineffective. It frames a complex issue as binary (good/bad), ignores the chapter's nuance (development benefits some, harms many), and offers no textual anchor. A strong opening would be: "The chapter forces us to ask: development for whom? The factory owners gain (para 6), but the river, the birds, and the poor lose. Let's discuss this asymmetry." A student who calls the weak opening "good" reveals they equate discussion with opinion-sharing, not evidence-based dialogue.

questions.q: Create a 2-minute role-play scenario where two characters from the chapter (e.g., the factory owner and the old farmer) debate the new highway construction. Write the opening lines for each.
questions.a: Factory owner: "भाई, यह सड़क नहीं, प्रगति की रेखा है। हमारे बच्चे शहर जाकर पढ़ेंगे, रोज़गार पाएंगे।" Old farmer: "सड़क तो बनी, पर मेरे खेत का पानी सूख गया। प्रगति उसकी होती है जिसके पास ज़मीन नहीं होती।" A poor answer gives both characters the same voice or ignores textual details (farmer's lost water, owner's 'progress' rhetoric) — showing the student hasn't internalized the chapter's class/ecology tensions.
